You should try the following : check your connection, disable ad-blocker, clear your browser cache, try in private mode, try from another browser/computer/connection. 0 The Ruhr: A Story of Coal Trade In 'The Ruhr: A Story of Coal Trade', the second game of Thomas Spitzer's historic coal trilogy, you are transported to the Ruhr region in the 18th century, at the beginning of the industrial revolution. the players transport and sell coal to cities and factories along the Ruhr river in the 18th and 19th centuries. By selling coal to cities and factories, players acquire unique progress markers. In the beginning, players have access only to low value coal. By selling coal to certain locations, players gain access to high value coal. In addition to selling coal, the players build warehouses, build locks, and export coal to neighboring countries in the pursuit of the most victory points. Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Note regarding Merchant: As discussed on the bug forum, the Merchant is ONLY activated when a development cube is awarded. A development cube is ONLY provided (at the cost of 1 thaler) if you deliver to a location that has an empty development field. A development cube is NOT awarded if you deliver to a location that has no empty development fields - in that case, you keep the 1 thaler, and the Merchant ability is NOT available to activate. [Rating: 4/10] This game is the essence of most of Spielworxx titles. Massively over priced, extemely mediocre production quality, unintelligable rule  book and inevitable printing errors and typos. It seems that Spielworxx has a very shallow pool of playtesters and no one who puts any effort into quality control. Thomas Spitzer deserved better.

[Rating: 5/10] A game that is more complex to learn how to play than it is to play well. Limited replayabiliy to boot.

[Rating: 5/10] The german rules of he first edition are confusing: "Naturfarbene Holzwürfel" when they really have the player colors; rule image showing a white meeple while it really is black. The rules are rather complex and the game felt long.

[Rating: 5/10] I believe the tech "tree" suggests a variability that isn't actually in the game since some advancements are vital and the choice is never between "this branch or that branch" but usually "which of these two first?" The rest of the game consists of a very simple sequence of actions with limited player influence interrupted only by potentially rather swingy random tile draws. Perhaps unsurprisingly, I think the game runs very long for this sort of game play.  I agree with those who say that Ruhrschifffahrt has a certain Wallace vibe. [Rating: 5/10] this game looks wonderfull but isn't worth its 70 euros. The game is too scenariobound, plays not logical enough and asks too many lookups in the rules.

[Rating: 5/10] A decent pick-up and deliver game that blends mechanics and theme (transporting coal along Germany's Ruhr river) well. Be forewarned - the random event selected each round can have a huge impact on player turns and tactics, which can be frustrating at times. Overall a solid, if unspectacular, game.

[Rating: 6/10] Feels a bit like a Martin Wallace game. Plays ok with three but I think four would be better. Some decent quirkiness, but the overall experience wasn't worth the additional cost of game and additional frustration of getting through the oddly organized rules. The actual game isn't hard to understand or teach once one person knows it though.  Ended up trading it with no real regrets. I would still happily play it if I run across it though.

[Rating: 6/10] Nice heavy Eurogame with a unique theme and unique mechanics. Sort of pick up and deliver, but in a different way than others in the genre. Dice represents the value of coal, which degrades when moving it along the river and around the locks. Delivering coal allows for players to "unlock" technologies which provide in-game bonuses or VPs.  I think they could have streamlined the new version a bit and made some of the iconography more clear. [Rating: 6/10] A nice game: original and thematic (much more than the average Euro). It is not difficult to play: rules are not difficult; even if the handbook has the fame not to be well written, I had no problem in learning the game, apart for minor things. It is replayable. The only (somehow not small) minus is that the choices offered, although interesting both at the strategic and at the tactical level, are too few (there is not a huge decision space as I prefer in games).
